subject: food-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Proteins are built from smaller units. What are these units called?
questions.explain: Proteins are made up of long chains of amino acids joined together.

questions.q: Which of these foods is a source of high biological value (HBV) protein?
questions.explain: Egg is an HBV protein because it supplies all of the essential amino acids the body needs.

questions.q: Why is an egg described as a high biological value (HBV) protein?
options: It contains all of the essential amino acids
It is missing one or more essential amino acids
It contains no essential amino acids
It is made only from fatty acids and glycerol
questions.explain: HBV proteins provide all the essential amino acids in the correct proportions for the body.

questions.q: Fats and oils are made up of glycerol combined with which units?
questions.explain: A fat molecule is formed from one glycerol unit joined to three fatty acids.

questions.q: Which type of carbohydrate is a complex (polysaccharide) carbohydrate that releases energy more slowly?
questions.explain: Starch is a complex carbohydrate broken down gradually, giving a slower, more sustained release of energy than sugars.

questions.q: A teenager wants to increase the fibre in their diet. Which swap would best achieve this?
options: Choosing wholemeal bread instead of white bread
Choosing full-fat milk instead of skimmed milk
Choosing butter instead of low-fat spread
Choosing sweets instead of fresh fruit
questions.explain: Wholemeal (wholegrain) products retain the bran, making them a good source of dietary fibre.

questions.q: Regularly eating too much saturated fat is most closely linked to which health problem?
options: Raised blood cholesterol and coronary heart disease
questions.explain: A high intake of saturated fat can raise blood cholesterol, increasing the risk of coronary heart disease.

questions.q: A diet high in free sugars is most strongly associated with which two health issues?
questions.explain: Frequent free-sugar intake promotes tooth decay and contributes to obesity and type 2 diabetes.

questions.q: What is the maximum recommended daily intake of salt for an adult?
questions.explain: Adults are advised to eat no more than 6g of salt per day.

questions.q: Why is eating too much salt a health concern?
options: It can raise blood pressure, increasing the risk of heart disease and stroke
It prevents the absorption of iron
questions.explain: A high salt intake is linked to high blood pressure (hypertension), a risk factor for strokes and heart disease.

questions.q: A middle-aged man has been advised to lower his risk of coronary heart disease. Which change is most appropriate?
options: Grill food and cut down on saturated fat
Increase his intake of butter and cream
Eat more processed and salty snacks
Add extra sugar to his drinks
questions.explain: Reducing saturated fat and using lower-fat cooking methods such as grilling helps lower CHD risk.

questions.q: Which group correctly lists the fat-soluble vitamins?
options: Vitamins A, D, E and K
questions.explain: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble, while the B vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble.

questions.q: Why is vitamin D important, and what does a deficiency cause in children?
options: It helps the body absorb calcium; deficiency causes rickets
It helps the blood clot; deficiency causes anaemia
It helps make haemoglobin; deficiency causes scurvy
It helps night vision; deficiency causes goitre
questions.explain: Vitamin D aids calcium absorption for strong bones, and a deficiency can cause rickets in children.

questions.q: A lack of which vitamin causes the deficiency disease scurvy?
questions.explain: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is needed to make collagen, and its deficiency leads to scurvy.

questions.q: How does vitamin C help maintain healthy iron levels in the body?
options: It helps the body absorb iron from food
It stores iron in the liver
It removes excess iron from the blood
questions.explain: Vitamin C improves the absorption of non-haem iron, helping to prevent iron-deficiency anaemia.

questions.q: Iron is needed to make which substance, and what does a deficiency cause?
questions.explain: Iron is essential for making haemoglobin in red blood cells, and a shortage causes anaemia.

questions.q: Which meal would best help a teenager absorb the most iron?
options: Beef stir-fry with peppers and a glass of orange juice
White pasta with butter and cheese
A cheese sandwich on white bread
questions.explain: The iron-rich beef combined with vitamin C from peppers and orange juice maximises iron absorption.

questions.q: How much energy does 1 gram of fat provide?
questions.explain: Fat is the most energy-dense macronutrient, providing about 9 kcal (37 kJ) per gram.

questions.q: What happens over time if a person regularly takes in more energy than they use?
options: They gain weight and may become overweight or obese
They lose weight and become underweight
Their energy balance stays exactly the same
questions.explain: When energy intake exceeds energy expenditure, the surplus is stored as fat, leading to weight gain.

questions.q: Using the estimated average requirement (EAR), roughly how much energy does an averagely active adult woman need each day?
questions.explain: The EAR for an average adult woman is about 2000 kcal per day, compared with about 2500 kcal for a man.
